Let $H$ be a hypergraph with edge ideal $I=I(H)$. Write $\alpha(I)$ for the least degree of a nonzero homogeneous element of $I$, and let $\operatorname{ht}(I)$ denote the height of $I$. A hypergraph is **$(a:b)$-partite** when it has the specific partite structure used to obtain the Waldschmidt lower bound $\widehat{\alpha}(I)\geq a/b$. **The partite-structure conjecture.** If $H$ has the packing property, then $H$ is

$$
(\alpha(I)\operatorname{ht}(I):\operatorname{ht}(I))\text{-partite}.
$$

The proposed structure would apply the lower bound $\widehat{\alpha}(I)\geq a/b$ with $a=\alpha(I)\operatorname{ht}(I)$ and $b=\operatorname{ht}(I)$, yielding $\widehat{\alpha}(I)\geq\alpha(I)$. Together with the general inequality $\widehat{\alpha}(I)\leq\alpha(I)$, this would prove equality for ideals with the packing property.

Let $d\geq 2$, let $v_d$ denote the volume of the unit ball in $\mathbb{R}^d$, and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ be a domain. For $c\in(0,1)$, let $L(\Omega,c)$ be the minimal length of a partition of $\Omega$ into two regions of prescribed volumes $c|\Omega|$ and $(1-c)|\Omega|$. For $n>1$ and ${\mathbf c}=(c_i)_{i=1}^n\in\mathbb{R}^n_+$ with $\sum_{i=1}^n c_i=1$, let $PL(\Omega,{\mathbf c})$ be the minimal perimeter of a partition into $n$ regions with prescribed volume fractions $c_i$. 

**Longest minimal length partition conjecture.** Given $c\in(0,1)$, the set $\Omega$ maximizing $L(\Omega,c)$ under the constraint $|\Omega|=v_d$ is the ball. Given $n>1$ and ${\mathbf c}=(c_i)_{i=1}^n\in\mathbb{R}^n_+$ with $\sum_{i=1}^n c_i=1$, the set $\Omega$ maximizing $PL(\Omega,{\mathbf c})$ under the constraint $|\Omega|=v_d$ is the ball.

The conjecture extends the equal-area results to partitions with prescribed, possibly unequal, volumes. Numerical simulations suggest that the disk in two dimensions and the ball in three dimensions maximize the minimal partition length or perimeter, but the general assertion remains open.

Let $K_n$ be the complete graph. The $d$-hyperconnectivity matroid $\mathcal H_n^d$ is a $\{K_{d+2},K_{d+1,d+1}\}$-matroid, $\mathcal I_n^2$ is a $\{K_5,K_{3,3}\}$-matroid, and $\mathcal R_n^d$ is a $\{K_{d+2},K_{d+2,d+2}\}$-matroid. **Valuation maximality conjecture.** (a) For $n\geq2d+2$, $\mathcal H_n^d$ is the unique maximal $\{K_{d+2},K_{d+1,d+1}\}$-matroid on $K_n$, and its rank function is $\operatorname{val}_{\{K_{d+2},K_{d+1,d+1}\}}$. (b) For $d=2$ and $n\geq6$, $\mathcal I_n^2$ is the unique maximal $\{K_5,K_{3,3}\}$-matroid on $K_n$, and its rank function is $\operatorname{val}_{\{K_5,K_{3,3}\}}$. (c) For $d\geq3$ and $n\geq2d+4$, $\mathcal R_n^d$ is the unique maximal $\{K_{d+2},K_{d+2,d+2}\}$-matroid on $K_n$, and its rank function is $\operatorname{val}_{\{K_{d+2},K_{d+2,d+2}\}}$. These are proposed strengthenings of the preceding maximality conjecture; no resolution is given in the supplied text.

Let $q \geq 5$ be an odd prime power, let $g=\gcd(n,q-1)$, and write the prime factorization of $g$ as $g=p_1^{r_1}\cdots p_s^{r_s}$. For a natural number $m$, write

$$
m=p_1^{a_1}\cdots p_s^{a_s}q_1^{b_1}\cdots q_t^{b_t}
$$

with the $p_i$ and $q_j$ distinct, and define

$$
m_{n,q}=p_1^{a_1}\cdots p_s^{a_s},\qquad T_{n,q}(m)=\sum_{i=1}^{t}q_i^{b_i}.
$$

Here $p({\rm GL}_n(\mathbb{F}_q))$ and $p({\rm SL}_n(\mathbb{F}_q))$ denote the minimal faithful permutation degrees. **General linear group conjecture.** If $g=1$, then

$$
p({\rm GL}_n(\mathbb{F}_q))=\frac{q^n-1}{q-1}+T_{n,q}(q-1),
$$

whereas if $g>1$, then

$$
p({\rm GL}_n(\mathbb{F}_q))=p({\rm SL}_n(\mathbb{F}_q))+T_{n,q}(q-1).
$$

These formulas predict the additional contribution from the factors of $q-1$ not appearing in $g$; the conjecture is presented as an explicit formula for general linear groups, with no resolution supplied in the source.

Let $m\geq 3$ be an integer, let $V=\{1,2,\dots,m-1\}$, and let $D^{(m,V)}$ denote the generating series for Dyck paths whose peaks avoid the heights in the congruence classes specified by $(m,V)$. Write $H(D^{(m,V)})$ for the sequence of Hankel determinants of this series.

**Extremal-set periodicity conjecture.** The sequence $H(D^{(m,V)})$ is periodic and has the form

$$
H\big(D^{(m,V)}\big)=\begin{cases} (1,\underbrace{0,\dots,0}_{m-2},1,1)^* & \text{if }m\equiv 1,2\pmod{4},\\ (1,\underbrace{0,\dots,0}_{m-2},-1,-1,-1,\underbrace{0,\dots,0}_{m-2},1,1)^* & \text{if }m\equiv 0,3\pmod{4}.
\end{cases}
$$

This gives an explicit periodic sequence for the extremal avoiding set. The paper presents this as part of its investigation of periodicity; the concluding remarks state that many periodic cases remain outside the sufficient condition and pose broader questions about characterizing all pairs $(m,V)$ with periodic $H(D^{(m,V)})$.

Let $k\ge 1$ and $a,b\ge 0$ satisfy $2k>a$ and $a+b\ge 2$. Define

$$
ch(a,b)\coloneqq\min\big\{q:(q+1)a+b\le 2^q\big\}.
$$

Set

$$
C\coloneqq\max\big\{ch(a,b),RU_0^k(2a+b)\big\},
$$

$$
\chi_0\coloneqq\max\big\{x:RU_1^k(x,a-x)\le C-1,\ x\le a,\ x\le k\big\},
$$

$$
\chi_1\coloneqq\max\big\{y:RU_1^k(\chi_0,y+a-\chi_0)\le C-1,\ y\le b,\ y\le k-\chi_0\big\}.
$$

**Meng–Lin–Yang's conjecture.** With these definitions,

$$
RU_1^k(a,b)=\max\big\{C,1+RU_1^k(a-\chi_0,b-\chi_1+\chi_0)\big\}.
$$

This conjecture concerns the optimal query in the Rényi-Ulam game with restricted-size queries, where $RU_1^k(a,b)$ denotes the relevant one-lie query complexity and the parameters describe the current state. The paper presents it as a conjecture about optimal play; no resolution is given in the supplied text.

The discussion concerns an $o$-minimal structure, a finite family of formulas $\Phi(x;y)$, distal density, and distal cell decompositions; here $\abs{x}$ denotes the length of the object-variable tuple. The preceding results give bounds such as distal cell-decomposition exponent $2\abs{x}-4$ for $\abs{x}\geq 4$ over the ordered field $\mathbb{R}$.

**Conjecture on optimal o-minimal bounds.** The same bounds should hold in any $o$-minimal structure, potentially via Davenport–Schinzel sequences. Moreover, every $\Phi(x;y)$ in an $o$-minimal structure should have distal density $\abs{x}$, or even admit a distal cell decomposition of exponent exactly $\abs{x}$.

These claims would improve the general bounds discussed in the paper and would require new tools; the source presents them as conjectural extensions of the known results over $\mathbb{R}$.

Let $\Gamma$ be a finite abelian group of order at least $2$, and let $\mathbb{F}$ be a finite field. A **$\Gamma$-graphic delta-matroid** is a delta-matroid associated with a $\Gamma$-gain graph; it is **representable over $\mathbb{F}$** when it admits a representation over $\mathbb{F}$. **Complete characterization conjecture.** Every $\Gamma$-graphic delta-matroid is representable over $\mathbb{F}$ if and only if

$$
(\Gamma,\mathbb{F})=(\mathbb{Z}_p^k,\operatorname{GF}(p^\ell))
$$

for some prime $p$ and positive integers $k\leq\ell$. The preceding results establish the sufficiency when $k\leq\ell$ and show that necessity requires $\Gamma$ to be an elementary abelian $p$-group and $\mathbb{F}$ to have characteristic $p$; the conjecture asserts that these conditions, together with $k\leq\ell$, give the complete characterization.

Let $K$ be a degree $d$ number field with ring of integers $O_K\cong\mathbb{Z}^d$, and let $p(x)\in K[x]$ be an $O_K$-valued intersective polynomial. **Finitary configuration conjecture.** For distinct nonzero $r,s\inO_K$, every $\delta,\varepsilon>0$ admits $N=N(\varepsilon,\delta)\in\mathbb{N}$ such that every set $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}^d$ with $|A|>\delta N^d$ contains at least $(\delta^3-\varepsilon)N^d$ configurations $\{x,x+rp(n),x+sp(n)\}$ for some $n\ne0$. Moreover, if $s/r\in\mathbb{Q}$, or more generally if no two conjugates of $s/r$ are negatives of each other, then the same conclusion holds with at least $(\delta^4-\varepsilon)N^d$ configurations of the form $\{x,x+rp(n),x+sp(n),x+rp(n)+sp(n)\}$. This is proposed as a finitary analogue of the preceding ergodic and combinatorial recurrence results; the supplied text does not establish either finitary assertion.

Let $p$ be an odd prime. For a $p$-uniform hypergraph with vertex set $\mathbb N$ and edge set $\mathcal F$, define

$$
\mathcal E(\mathcal F)=\{\mathbf e_F:F\in\mathcal F\}\subseteq\mathbb F_p^\omega,
$$

where $\mathbf e_F=\sum_{n\in F}\mathbf e_n$. The **chromatic number** of a hypergraph is the least number of colors in a vertex coloring for which no edge is monochromatic, or infinity if no finite coloring exists. The Cayley graph $\operatorname{Cay}(\mathbb F_p^\omega,\mathcal E(\mathcal F))$ has vertex set $\mathbb F_p^\omega$ and edges whose differences lie in $\mathcal E(\mathcal F)$ or its negatives.

**Hypergraph-to-Cayley conjecture.** If the hypergraph with edge set $\mathcal F$ has infinite chromatic number, then

$$
\operatorname{Cay}(\mathbb F_p^\omega,\mathcal E(\mathcal F))
$$

has infinite chromatic number.

For each fixed odd prime $p$, this conjecture is stated as equivalent in the paper to the corresponding finite-field recurrence conjecture. Its general validity remains open.

Let $M=(M_{n,k})_{n,k\geq 0}$ be the array associated with the row numerators of the generating functions of $T(n,m)$. For a fixed column $k$, write its generating function as $\sum_{n\geq 0}M_{n,k}x^n$, and let $N_4(x)$ be the polynomial displayed below.

**First-five-column conjecture.** The generating functions for columns $0,1,2,3,4$ of $M$, in that order, are

$$
\frac{1}{1-x},\qquad \frac{1}{(1-x)^2(1-x-x^2)},
$$

$$
\frac{1-x^2-x^3-x^4+x^5}{(1-x)^3(1-x-x^2)^2(1-2x-x^2+x^3)},
$$

$$
\frac{1+x-6x^2-15x^3+21x^4+35x^5-13x^6-51x^7+3x^8+21x^9+5x^{10}+x^{11}-5x^{12}-x^{13}-x^{14}}{(1-x)^4(1-x-x^2)^3(1-2x-x^2+x^3)^2(1-2x-3x^2+x^3+x^4)},
$$

and

$$
\frac{N_4(x)}{(1-x)^5(1-x-x^2)^4(1-2x-x^2+x^3)^3(1-2x-3x^2+x^3+x^4)^2(1-3x-3x^2+4x^3+x^4-x^5)},
$$

where

$$
\begin{aligned}
N_4(x)={}&1+4x-31x^2-67x^3+348x^4+418x^5-1893x^6-1084x^7+4326x^8+4295x^9-7680x^{10}-9172x^{11}+9104x^{12}\\
&+11627x^{13}-5483x^{14}-10773x^{15}+1108x^{16}+7255x^{17}+315x^{18}-3085x^{19}-228x^{20}+669x^{21}+102x^{22}\\
&-23x^{23}-45x^{24}-16x^{25}+11x^{26}+2x^{27}-x^{28}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The claim records explicit rational generating functions for the first five columns of $M$. It is an empirical conjecture associated with OEIS sequence A205497, and the supplied material gives no evidence that it has been proved.

Let $f$ be a mapping from $\{1,2,\ldots,n\}$ to subsets of $\{1,2,\ldots,n\}$ such that

$$
\bigcup_{i=1}^n f(i)=\{1,2,\ldots,n\}.
$$

For a finite set $A\subseteq\mathbb{N}$, define

$$
\operatorname{conv}f(A)=\{\min f(A),\ldots,\max f(A)\},
$$

the convex hull of $f(A)$. Let $I_1,\ldots,I_k$ be any partition of $\{1,2,\ldots,n\}$ into consecutive blocks,

$$
I_1=\{1,2,\ldots,i_1\},\quad I_2=\{i_1+1,\ldots,i_2\},\quad \ldots,\quad I_k=\{i_{k-1}+1,\ldots,n\}.
$$

**Discrete convex-hull conjecture.** There exist $j\in\{1,2,\ldots,k\}$ and $r,s\in I_j$ such that, for some $l\leq k$,

$$
(\operatorname{conv}f)^l(\{r,s\})\supseteq\{r,s\}.
$$

The paper proposes this conjecture as a discrete statement implying the covering-system conjecture; its general status is not resolved in the supplied text.

Fix $w\in S_n$. A **heavy climbing chain** of $w$ is a climbing chain together with its marked-link data $M(C)$; write its overlined and ordinary weights as $\operatorname{\overline{wt}}(C,M(C))$ and $\operatorname{wt}(C,M(C))$. Let $C^S(w)$ be the staircase climbing chain and set $\xi=(C^S(w),M(C^S(w)))$. **Staircase heavy-chain conjecture.** For any term order satisfying $x_1>x_2>\cdots>x_n$, 
$$
\bm{x}^{\operatorname{\overline{wt}}(\xi)}=\min\left\\{\bm{x}^{\operatorname{\overline{wt}}(C,M(C))}\mid C\text{ is a heavy climbing chain of }w\right\\}.
$$
 Equivalently, 
$$
\bm{x}^{\operatorname{wt}(\xi)}=\max\left\\{\bm{x}^{\operatorname{wt}(C,M(C))}\mid C\text{ is a heavy climbing chain of }w\right\\}.
$$
 This conjecture identifies the staircase chain as extremal among heavy climbing chains for the reverse variable order; the source reports verification for $n\leq 8$, while a general proof remains open.

Let $\mathcal{D}$ be the partial order of finite directed graphs under the substructure relation $\sqsubseteq$. Let $\operatorname{Aut}\mathcal{D}$ denote its automorphism group, and let $\mathcal{C}$ be the subgroup generated by the explicitly constructed automorphisms $\varphi_i$, whose structure is

$$
\mathcal{C}\cong(\mathbb{Z}_2^4\times S_4)\rtimes_{\alpha}\mathbb{Z}_2.
$$

Here $S_4$ is the symmetric group on $\{A,B,C,D\}$, and $\alpha$ is defined by

$$
\alpha(0)=\operatorname{id},\qquad \alpha(1):(p,q,r,s,\pi)\mapsto(q,p,s,r,(BC)\pi(BC)).
$$

**The automorphism group conjecture.**

$$
\operatorname{Aut}\mathcal{D}\cong\mathcal{C}\cong(\mathbb{Z}_2^4\times S_4)\rtimes_{\alpha}\mathbb{Z}_2.
$$

Thus the automorphism group of the substructure ordering would have exactly $768$ elements, and the conjecture asserts that the constructed subgroup contains all automorphisms of the partial order. The paper proves the stated structure of $\mathcal{C}$ but does not prove that no additional automorphisms exist.

For a graph $G$, write $f_G(r)$ for its growth function, and let $G\boxtimes H$ denote the strong product of graphs $G$ and $H$. Let $K_t$ be the complete graph on $t$ vertices. A graph has polynomial growth with parameters $c$ and $d$ when $f_G(r)\leqslant cr^d$, and each $T_i$ below is a tree with growth bounded linearly in $r$.

**Polynomial-growth product-structure conjecture.** There exist functions $g\colon\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ and $h\colon\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{R}$ such that for any $c\geqslant 1$ and $d\in\mathbb{N}$, every graph $G$ with growth $f_G(r)\leqslant cr^d$ is isomorphic to a subgraph of

$$
T_1\boxtimes\cdots\boxtimes T_d\boxtimes K_{g(c,d)},
$$

where each $T_i$ is a tree of growth $f_{T_i}(r)\leqslant h(c,d)r$.

This is presented as a more general rough characterisation of graphs of polynomial growth, extending the preceding linear-growth conjecture. Its status is unresolved in the supplied source.

Let $G$ be a finite group, let $A\subset G$, and suppose that $A$ is both $t$-independent and $s$-spanning, with $t$ even. Write $m=t/2$ and define the Delannoy numbers by

$$
a(m,s)=\sum_{i\geq 0}{s\choose i}{m\choose i}2^i.
$$

A set is **perfect** when equality occurs in the bounds of the preceding theorem, namely when the relevant cardinality equality holds. **The perfect-set classification conjecture.** The only instances of perfect sets in $G$ are the three cases listed: $s=1$ with $|G|=2m+1$ and $A,-A$ partitioning $G\setminus\{0\}$; $m=1$ with $G$ cyclic of order $2s+1$ and $A=\{a\}$ where $\gcd(a,|G|)=1$; or $m=2$ with $G$ cyclic of order $2s^2+2s+1$ and $A=c\cdot\{s,s+1\}$ where $\gcd(c,|G|)=1$. In particular, one must have $s=1$ or $m\in\{1,2\}$. The conjecture proposes completeness of the short classification of equality cases for the independent-spanning-set bounds. The supplied status evidence treats related questions as open, and no resolution of this classification is given.

Let $p$ and $q$ be distinct odd primes with $q>2\sqrt p$ and Legendre symbol $\left(\frac pq\right)=1$, let $G_q=\operatorname{PSL}_2(\mathbb{F}_q)$, and let $S_{p,q}\subset G_q$ be the subset of cardinality $p+1$ arising from the Lubotzky–Phillips–Sarnak Ramanujan graph construction. Let $Y_{S_{p,q},k}$ be the associated balanced Cayley complex, and let $h_{k-1}$ denote its $(k-1)$-st coboundary expansion constant. **Coboundary expansion conjecture for Ramanujan balanced Cayley complexes.** For any fixed $k\geq 1$ there exist constants $p_0(k)<\infty$ and $\epsilon_0(k)>0$ such that if $p>p_0(k)$, $q>2\sqrt p$ and $\left(\frac pq\right)=1$, then

$$
h_{k-1}\left(Y_{S_{p,q},k}\right)\geq\epsilon_0(k).
$$

This is proposed as a coboundary-expansion analogue of the established spectral-gap estimate for these complexes. The source gives no resolution of the conjecture.

Let $F$ be the set of the following 13 partitions:

$$
\begin{gathered}
(1,1,1),(2,1,1),(2,2,1),(3,2,1),(3,3,1),(5,3,3),(4,4,1,1),\\
(5,4,1,1),(5,4,2,1),(5,5,2,1),(6,5,3,1,1),(6,6,3,1,1),(7,6,4,2,1).
\end{gathered}
$$

Define

$$
I_1=\{(1),(5,4,2,2),(9,8,6,4,2,2)\},\quad I_2=\{(1,1),(2,2),(4,3,1)\},
$$

$$
I_3=\{(1,1),(2,1),(2,2),(3,2),(3,3),(4,3,1),(4,4,1),(5,4,2),(6,5,3,1)\}.
$$

For $1\leq a\leq3$, let $\mathsf L_a$ be the set of partitions that do not begin with any $\boldsymbol c\in I_a$ and do not match $(b_1+k,\ldots,b_p+k)$ for any $(b_1,\ldots,b_p)\in F$ and $k\geq0$. **Kanade–Russell conjecture modulo 16.** The partition sets satisfy

$$
\mathsf L_1\stackrel{\mathsf{PT}}{\sim}T^{(16)}_{2,3,4,5,11,12,13,14},\qquad
\mathsf L_2\stackrel{\mathsf{PT}}{\sim}T^{(2)}_1,
$$

$$
\mathsf L_3\stackrel{\mathsf{PT}}{\sim}T^{(16)}_{1,4,6,7,9,10,12,15}.
$$

The restrictions exclude specified initial subpartitions and translated patterns, while the right-hand sides impose congruence conditions on all parts. The source presents these identities as a conjectural example connected with vertex-operator bases; their resolution status is not specified here.

Let $\mathbf{N}_{3,n}$ be the Newton polytope, and let $\gamma_{j_1,j_2,j_3}$ be the generalized positive root

$$
\gamma_{j_1,j_2,j_3}=\sum_{t=j_1}^{j_2-2}\alpha_{1,t}+\sum_{t=j_2-1}^{j_3-3}\alpha_{2,t}.
$$

Assume that $\{j_1,j_2,j_3\}$ is totally nonfrozen, meaning that no two indices are cyclically adjacent. The generalized positive roots are linear functions on $\mathbb{R}^{2\times(n-3)}$.

**Eight-face conjecture.** The facet of $\mathbf{N}_{3,n}$ minimizing $\gamma_{j_1,j_2,j_3}$ has exactly eight codimension-$3$ faces combinatorially isomorphic to

$$
\mathbf{N}_{3,j_2-j_1+2}\times\mathbf{N}_{3,j_3-j_2+2}\times\mathbf{N}_{3,j_1-j_3+n+2}.
$$

These faces correspond to the eight weakly separated collections listed in the source. The claim generalizes the observed three-split structure and remains unproved in the supplied text.

A poset has a **planar diagram** if its cover graph can be drawn in the plane with every cover relation represented by a curve directed upwards. Its **cover graph** is the graph whose vertices are the elements of the poset and whose edges join pairs in a cover relation. The dimension of a poset $P$, denoted $\dim(P)$, is the least number of linear extensions whose intersection is $P$. A class of posets is **dim-bounded** if the dimensions of its members are bounded by a function of the relevant structural parameter—in particular, here by an absolute constant for the stated class. **The planar-poset dim-boundedness conjectures.** (1) The class of posets with planar diagrams is dim-bounded. (2) The class of posets with planar cover graphs is dim-bounded. These statements address whether planarity, despite allowing posets of arbitrarily large dimension in known constructions, forces dimension to remain bounded. The paper discusses the longstanding problem and notes that the planar cover-graph case is pursued through results forcing large standard examples; the supplied text does not establish either assertion.
